questions.stem: A footnote in the planner's memo describes a federal note whose face left the value unfilled. Explain the arrangement and what it allowed.

answer.exemplar: The note was printed with the denomination left blank, and the paying cashier filled in the value and signed the note when it was handed out. One printing plate therefore served several small denominations, which let the Treasury supply everyday change without ordering a separate plate and press run for every amount from two and a half cents up to fifty cents.

questions.explanation: Leaving the value blank let one plate serve several denominations, so the Treasury could supply small change quickly. The arrangement was a convenience in printing, not a change in what the note was worth.
questions.hint: Think about the printing side of the arrangement.

options.text: A way to tighten credit in easy times and loosen the pressure in tight ones, without waiting for a new statute.
A way to give member banks the right to set their own requirement after a period of good business.
options.misconception: Turns a central power into a bank option

options.text: A way to abolish reserves entirely if the Board found the gold cover excessive.
options.misconception: Reads the flexibility as a licence to abolish

options.text: A way to let the states lower the requirement below the national figure when times were hard.
options.misconception: Invents a state power over the requirement

questions.explanation: A variable requirement let the central board answer conditions promptly, which is why the act gave it power to raise and lower it. A bank option, a licence to abolish, and a state power miss the intent.
questions.hint: Think about responding to changing conditions quickly.

questions.topic: The trouble a corner in one share created
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table of clearing house certificates issued during a crisis.
questions.stem: The memo's table of clearing house certificates lists an amount issued during the crisis. What does it show?

options.text: That the clearing houses pooled private metal to steady member banks, rather than waiting on the federal government.
That the federal government had already created the reserve banks and lent them gold.
options.misconception: Moves the rescue forward to the new reserve system

options.text: That the certificates were a permanent currency issued by the clearing houses for circulation.
options.misconception: Turns a certificate into circulating currency

options.text: That no private cooperation was possible, so the amount was raised by law.
options.misconception: Denies the private pooling the amount shows

questions.explanation: The certificates show member banks pooling their own resources through the clearing houses to meet withdrawals, which is why the crisis eased before any federal system existed. Federal lending or lasting currency misreads them.
questions.hint: Ask who supplied the metal behind the certificates.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The purchase that was stopped and the notes it left behind
questions.learningObjective: Explain the convenience of issuing paper against purchased silver.
questions.stem: The memo describes silver notes issued against metal the government bought. Explain why issuing paper against purchased silver was convenient.

answer.exemplar: Buying metal took time, and shipping bullion from the western mines to the eastern mints cost money and delayed the coinage that buyers of silver actually wanted. Issuing notes against the metal in the Treasury's keeping delivered the same claim on value immediately, in a form that travelled easily, while the silver itself waited for the mint.

questions.explanation: Paper against metal on hand gave buyers a claim on the silver without waiting for slow shipments and costly coinage. The notes were convenient instruments, which is why their status became so contested.
questions.hint: Compare the speed of paper with the speed of shipping metal.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a stopgap act was meant to bridge
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that actually belonged to the 1908 measure.
questions.stem: The memo's list of the 1908 measure's features includes several items. Which belong to it?

options.text: A commission to study the money system and authority to issue emergency notes during a crisis.
The creation of twelve reserve banks with a board of governors over them.
options.misconception: Attributes the reserve banks to the 1908 measure

options.text: The end of the note tax on state banks, which the states had fought for a generation.
options.misconception: Invents a note tax repeal in 1908

options.text: A permanent hundred percent gold cover for all circulating notes.
options.misconception: Invents a full gold cover requirement

questions.explanation: The 1908 measure provided a study commission and emergency notes for a crisis. The reserve banks, a note tax repeal, and a full gold cover came later or never came at all.
questions.hint: Keep the temporary measure separate from the permanent one.

questions.topic: The trouble a corner in one share created
questions.learningObjective: Order the crisis events as the memo's account presents them.
questions.stem: Sequence the memo's account of 1907: the corner, the bank's failure, the suspension of gold payments, and the clearing house rule.

options.text: The corner, the bank's failure, the suspension of gold payments, then the clearing house rule.
The corner, the suspension of gold payments, the bank's failure, then the clearing house rule.
options.misconception: Swaps the failure and the suspension

options.text: The bank's failure, the corner, the clearing house rule, then the suspension of gold payments.
options.misconception: Swaps the corner and the failure

options.text: The clearing house rule, the corner, the bank's failure, then the suspension of gold payments.
options.misconception: Starts with the rule that came last

questions.explanation: The corner came first, the bank closed next, the city stopped paying in gold for several days, and the clearing house rule restored orderly settlement. Every other order breaks the chain of causes.
questions.hint: Each event should explain the one after it.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The weight the country fixed for a dollar of gold
questions.learningObjective: Derive the ratio between metals from the quoted statutory weights.

stimulus.body: The silver dollar shall contain three hundred and seventy-one grains and a quarter of pure silver, and the gold dollar shall contain twenty-four grains and three quarters of pure gold.

questions.stem: The memo quotes the coinage act's silver definition. What does the quoted weight show about the ratio between metals?

options.text: That the metals stood in a definite proportion, since the same dollar held far more silver than gold by weight.
That the two metals were given equal weight within the same dollar.
options.misconception: Claims the quoted weights are identical

options.text: That the silver weight was set by whatever the mint could melt down that month.
options.misconception: Invents a monthly mint determination

options.text: That gold was worth more per grain than silver, since it occupied the smaller share of the dollar.
options.misconception: Confuses weight with value

questions.explanation: The quoted weights place far more silver than gold in one dollar, which is how a fixed proportion between metals was expressed. Equal weights, a monthly mint choice, and value from weight each misread it.
questions.hint: Compare the two numbers before judging value.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The trouble a corner in one share created
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a banker's letter describing the suspension of gold payments.

stimulus.body: We could not pay our depositors in gold this week, and we ask the clearing house to extend the arrangement so that business may continue upon credit.

questions.stem: A banker's letter quoted in the memo describes the week when gold payments were refused. What does the letter show?

options.text: That the strain was being managed by agreement among the banks, with credit standing in for coin during the panic.
That the government had ordered all payments made in paper and forbade gold payments by law.
options.misconception: Turns a private agreement into a federal order

options.text: That the banks had permanently abandoned the gold standard before any reform was debated.
options.misconception: Treats a temporary suspension as a permanent break

options.text: That only one bank was affected, since no other house had yet refused to pay in coin.
options.misconception: Restricts the refusal to a single institution

questions.explanation: The letter shows banks arranging among themselves to keep business going on credit while coin payments were suspended. A federal order, a permanent break, and one institution misread it.
questions.hint: Ask who was making the arrangements in this letter.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The date a statute fixed for redeeming paper
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the memo's account of why paper notes were issued during the war.
questions.stem: The memo's summary of wartime finance links paper notes to the war effort. What does it argue?

options.text: That issuing federal notes was the practical way to meet heavy wartime payments without waiting on taxes or coin.
That the notes were issued only to conceal the weakness of the government's credit with the public.
options.misconception: Makes issuance a pure deception

options.text: That the notes were unpopular and accepted only because the law forced people to take them.
options.misconception: Assumes acceptance came only from compulsion

options.text: That the government had already decided to abandon coin payments permanently after the war.
options.misconception: Invents a decided postwar abandonment

questions.explanation: The summary argues practicality: heavy wartime payments had to be met and notes could be issued at once, while tax money came slowly. Pure deception, compulsion alone, and a settled postwar plan misread it.
questions.hint: Look for the practical problem the notes solved.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The weight the country fixed for a dollar of gold
questions.learningObjective: State the standard established by a pair of statutory metal weights.
questions.stem: Read the gold weight line, then the silver weight line, and state the relationship the two entries set.

options.text: They set a proportion between the metals, with the same dollar holding many times more silver by weight than gold.
They set a preference, since only the gold entry was to be used in practice after the first decade.
options.misconception: Makes one entry a mere formality in practice

options.text: They set a ceiling on the silver the government would hold, since a dollar could not exceed a fixed weight.
options.misconception: Misreads the weights as a holding limit

options.text: They set nothing at all, since each entry described a separate coin with its own market value.
options.misconception: Denies the standard the pair establishes

questions.explanation: Two weights against one dollar are a standard, and the gap between them is the proportion the country set. A practical preference, a holding ceiling, and two unrelated coins misread the pair.
questions.hint: One unit, two metals, therefore a proportion.
